topics.title: How sleep works
topics.dek: The 90-minute cycle, the two clocks and what actually helps

slides.h: A night is four to six laps
slides.p: Sleep runs in cycles of roughly 90 minutes: light sleep, deep slow-wave sleep, then REM, where most vivid dreaming happens. Deep sleep dominates the first half of the night; REM stretches out toward morning. Cutting the night short mostly cuts REM.

slides.h: Deep sleep repairs; REM files
slides.p: Slow-wave sleep is when growth hormone is released, tissue repairs and the brain clears metabolic waste. REM is when memories are consolidated and emotions processed. You need both, which is why a full night beats a long nap.

slides.h: Two clocks decide when you're sleepy
slides.p: Sleep pressure (adenosine) builds the longer you're awake; caffeine blocks it. The circadian clock, set by light, makes you alert in the morning and drowsy at night regardless. You fall asleep easily when both say yes, at your usual bedtime after a full day awake.

slides.h: Seven to nine hours, for most adults
slides.p: Large studies put the sweet spot for adults at seven to nine hours; teenagers need eight to ten and sleep later by biology, not laziness. Short sleepers who 'do fine on five' mostly aren't: the deficit shows in reaction tests even when they feel okay.

slides.h: Light is the lever
slides.p: Bright light in the morning, ideally outdoors within an hour of waking, anchors the clock and makes the next night's sleep come earlier. Dim light in the evening lets melatonin rise. Screens matter less for their blue light than for keeping you alert and awake.

slides.h: Same wake time, every day
slides.p: A fixed wake time, including weekends, does more than any gadget. Sleeping in by three hours on Saturday is a time-zone shift the clock has to undo on Monday ('social jet lag'). If you must catch up, nap early and short: 20 minutes, before 3 p.m.

v.c: wake time, seven days a week; the clock sets itself from it

slides.h: Caffeine, alcohol and the cool room
slides.p: Caffeine's half-life is about five hours, so a 4 p.m. coffee is a half-dose at 9 p.m. Alcohol makes you fall asleep faster and then fragments the second half of the night, cutting REM. Keep the room cool (about 65–68 °F / 18–20 °C); core temperature has to drop to sleep.

items: A nightcap as a sleep aid
Big meals or hard workouts right before bed

slides.h: If you can't sleep, get up
slides.p: Lying awake teaches the brain that bed is where you worry. After about twenty minutes, get up, do something dull in dim light, and return when sleepy. Chronic insomnia responds best to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I), which works better than pills over time.

items: Back to bed only when sleepy
Still bad after weeks? Ask about CBT-I

quiz.why: Light, deep and REM sleep repeat roughly every 90 minutes, four to six times a night.

quiz.q: Cutting a night from eight hours to five mostly loses…
a: Neither; sleep just gets more efficient
quiz.why: Deep sleep is front-loaded; REM stretches out toward morning, so it's the part the alarm removes.

quiz.q: The single most effective habit for better sleep is…
a: A fixed wake time every day
A glass of wine before bed
quiz.why: The clock sets itself from when you wake and see light. Weekend lie-ins are a self-inflicted time-zone change.

take: 90-minute cycles; deep sleep early, REM late. Seven to nine hours.
Morning light and a fixed wake time anchor the clock.
Caffeine's half-life is five hours; alcohol wrecks the second half of the night.

topics.title: How vaccines train the immune system
topics.dek: Two lines of defense, memory cells and herd immunity

slides.h: The first line is general-purpose
slides.p: Skin, mucus, stomach acid and fever block or slow most invaders. If something gets through, innate immune cells attack anything that looks foreign within hours. It's fast and broad, but it doesn't learn, which is why a second cold is just as miserable as the first.

slides.h: The second line is specific, and slow the first time
slides.p: The adaptive system builds antibodies and T cells that fit one particular pathogen. The first time it meets a new germ, that takes a week or two, while you are sick. Afterward it keeps memory cells that respond in days the next time, often before you notice.

slides.h: A vaccine is a safe first meeting
slides.p: It shows the adaptive system a harmless version or piece of the germ (killed, weakened, a protein, or mRNA instructions to make one protein) so the slow first response happens without the disease. When the real thing arrives, the memory cells are already there.

slides.h: Side effects are the training in progress
slides.p: A sore arm, tiredness or a day of mild fever are the immune system doing what it was asked to do, not the disease. Serious reactions are rare and monitored. Nothing in a vaccine can cause the illness it prevents except a few live vaccines in people with weakened immunity, who are screened.

slides.h: Why some need boosters
slides.p: Memory fades at different rates. Measles protection lasts a lifetime after two doses; tetanus needs a top-up every ten years; flu mutates so fast that last year's memory doesn't fit this year's virus. Boosters remind the system or update it.

slides.h: Herd immunity protects the people who can't be
slides.p: When enough people are immune, a germ can't find its next host and chains of infection break. The threshold depends on how contagious the disease is: about 95 percent for measles, lower for less contagious ones. Newborns and people on chemotherapy rely on everyone else.

slides.h: What vaccines have done
slides.p: Smallpox killed about 300 million people in the 20th century; it was eradicated in 1980. Polio is down more than 99 percent since 1988. Measles deaths fell by more than 80 percent between 2000 and 2017. These are the largest public-health numbers there are.

slides.h: Keeping your own system in shape
slides.p: There's no supplement that 'boosts' immunity; the things that help are the dull ones. Sleep (people sleeping under six hours catch more colds), moving most days, not smoking, enough protein and vegetables, washing hands, and staying up to date on the shots your doctor recommends for your age.

a: Killing germs already in the body
Letting the adaptive immune system meet a harmless version first
Replacing the immune system for a year
quiz.why: The slow first response happens safely, leaving memory cells ready for the real pathogen.

quiz.q: A sore arm and tiredness the day after a shot are…
quiz.why: Mild, short reactions are the system responding. Serious reactions are rare and are why you wait fifteen minutes.

quiz.q: Measles needs about what share of a community immune to stop spreading?
quiz.why: Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known, so its herd-immunity threshold is very high.

take: Innate immunity is fast and general; adaptive immunity is specific and remembers.
A vaccine is the first meeting without the illness; side effects are the training.
Herd immunity protects those who can't be vaccinated; for measles that takes about 95%.

topics.title: What caffeine does
topics.dek: How it keeps you awake, how long it lasts and how much is too much

slides.h: It blocks the sleepy signal
slides.p: Adenosine builds up in the brain while you're awake and makes you drowsy. Caffeine fits the same receptors without activating them, so the signal is muffled. The adenosine is still there, piling up behind the blockade, which is why the crash arrives when the caffeine wears off.

slides.h: Half of it is still there five hours later
slides.p: Caffeine's half-life averages about five hours in healthy adults, ranging from three to seven by genetics, and much longer in pregnancy and with some medications. A 200 mg coffee at 3 p.m. leaves about 100 mg at 8 p.m. and 50 mg at 1 a.m.

slides.h: How much is in what
slides.p: Numbers vary by brew and brand: a home drip coffee is about 95 mg a cup, espresso about 65 mg a shot, black tea 45, green tea 30, a cola 35, an energy drink 80 to 300. 'Decaf' still has 2 to 15 mg.

slides.h: 400 mg a day, for most healthy adults
slides.p: That's the FDA's figure for an amount not generally linked to harm: about four cups of coffee. Pregnancy guidance is 200 mg. Children and teens should have little or none. Energy drinks are the usual way people blow past it without noticing.

slides.h: The benefits are real, and modest
slides.p: Caffeine improves reaction time, alertness and endurance performance, and habitual moderate coffee drinking is associated with lower risk of several diseases in large observational studies. It also raises heart rate and blood pressure briefly and can worsen anxiety and reflux.

a: associations with lower risk of type 2 diabetes, Parkinson's

slides.h: Tolerance and withdrawal
slides.p: Regular use grows more adenosine receptors, so the same dose does less; the morning cup then mostly reverses overnight withdrawal rather than adding alertness. Stopping suddenly brings headaches and fatigue for two to nine days. Taper by a cup every few days instead.

items: Days 1–3: swap one cup for half-caf or tea
Resume at a lower dose, or not

slides.h: Timing it well
slides.p: Delay the first coffee until an hour or so after waking, when the natural cortisol rise has done its work. Keep the last one eight to ten hours before bed. A 'coffee nap' (drink, then nap 20 minutes while it kicks in) is the sharpest afternoon trick there is.

items: it's not a diuretic for regulars

slides.h: When to be careful
slides.p: Pregnancy, heart rhythm problems, anxiety disorders, reflux, insomnia and some medications (certain antibiotics, oral contraceptives) all change the calculus. Pure caffeine powder has killed people: a teaspoon is roughly 28 cups of coffee. Energy drinks plus alcohol hide how drunk you are.

items: Arrhythmia or anxiety: talk to a clinician

a: Blocking the receptors adenosine uses to signal sleepiness
quiz.why: The sleepiness signal is muffled, not removed. When the caffeine clears, the built-up adenosine hits at once.

quiz.q: After a 200 mg coffee at 3 p.m., roughly how much is still in you at 8 p.m.?
quiz.why: The average half-life is about five hours, so half remains, and a quarter at 1 a.m.

quiz.q: The FDA's guideline for healthy adults is up to about…
quiz.why: About four cups of coffee. Pregnancy guidance is 200 mg; children should have little or none.

take: It blocks adenosine; the crash is the backlog arriving.
Half-life about five hours: last coffee eight to ten hours before bed.
400 mg a day for most adults, 200 in pregnancy; energy drinks add up fast.

topics.title: Exercise: zones, minutes and strength
topics.dek: The 150-minute guideline, heart-rate zones and the talk test

slides.h: The guideline fits on one line
slides.p: At least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity (or 75 vigorous), plus muscle-strengthening work on two days. Spread however you like; even bouts of a few minutes count. Going from nothing to a little is the step with the biggest health payoff.

slides.h: Moderate and vigorous, by the talk test
slides.p: Moderate: you can talk but not sing (brisk walk, easy cycling). Vigorous: you can say a few words before needing a breath (running, hard cycling, singles tennis). No device needed; the test tracks heart rate closely enough for anyone who isn't training for a race.

b: a few words at a time

slides.h: Estimating your maximum heart rate
slides.p: The rough rule is 220 minus your age: about 180 for a 40-year-old. It's an average with a wide spread; your real max may be 10 or more beats either way. Zones based on it are approximate, which is fine for health. Athletes test it properly.

slides.h: The five zones
slides.p: Zone 1 is recovery; zone 2 (roughly 60–70 percent of max) is the long, conversational effort that builds the aerobic engine and burns the most fat per minute; zones 3–4 build pace and lactate tolerance; zone 5 is short all-out intervals. Most training for most people belongs in zone 2.

slides.h: Strength is not optional
slides.p: Muscle mass falls from around age 30 and faster after 60. Two sessions a week of the big movements (squat, hinge, push, pull, carry) preserve it, protect bones, joints and blood sugar, and are the strongest predictor of staying independent later. Bodyweight counts.

slides.h: Resting heart rate is a free report card
slides.p: A normal adult resting pulse is about 60 to 100; fit people often sit in the 50s. As you train, yours drifts down. A morning pulse 7 to 10 beats above your usual is an early sign of overtraining, poor sleep or an illness coming on. Measure it before getting up.

slides.h: Recovery is where you get fitter
slides.p: The workout is the stress; the adaptation happens afterward, during sleep and easy days. Hard days need easy days after them. Soreness that lasts more than three days, a rising resting pulse or getting slower while training harder all mean back off, not push through.

slides.h: Starting from zero
slides.p: Walk. Ten minutes after meals, then twenty, then brisk. Add two days of chair stands, wall push-ups and a band. Build over weeks, not days; the injuries happen when enthusiasm outruns tendons. Anyone with heart disease, chest pain or dizziness on exertion should check in with a clinician first.

items: Month 2+: one harder session a week

quiz.q: The weekly guideline for adults is…
a: An hour of vigorous exercise daily
quiz.why: 150 moderate or 75 vigorous minutes, plus muscle work on two days. Any amount above zero already helps.

quiz.q: During moderate exercise you should be able to…
a: Say only a word or two
quiz.why: That's the talk test. A few words at a time means vigorous; singing means easy.

quiz.q: A morning resting pulse 10 beats above your usual most likely means…
a: You need more recovery or you're getting sick
quiz.why: Resting heart rate falls with fitness; a jump is an early warning of overtraining, poor sleep or illness.

take: 150 moderate minutes a week plus two strength days; the talk test sets the intensity.
Most training time belongs in the easy, conversational zone.
Strength preserves independence; recovery is where fitness is built.

topics.title: First aid: the five things to know
topics.dek: CPR, choking, bleeding, burns and when to call

slides.h: Call first, or call fast
slides.p: An unresponsive adult who isn't breathing normally: call emergency services (911 in the U.S.) or have someone call, and send someone for an AED. Put the phone on speaker; dispatchers talk you through everything on these cards. These are reminders, not a substitute for a course.

items: Not breathing normally? Call 911, get an AED

slides.h: CPR: push hard, push fast
slides.p: Heel of one hand on the center of the chest, other hand on top, arms straight. Push at least 2 inches deep, 100 to 120 times a minute (the beat of 'Stayin' Alive'), letting the chest fully rise between pushes. Hands-only CPR is recommended for untrained bystanders with adults.

v.c: compressions a minute, at least 2 inches deep, center of the chest

slides.h: The AED does the thinking
slides.p: Turn it on and do what it says. It reads the heart rhythm and shocks only if a shock will help. Attach the pads to bare skin where the pictures show, make sure nobody is touching the person, press the button if told, then go straight back to compressions.

slides.h: Choking: ask, then act
slides.p: Can they cough or speak? Encourage coughing and stay close. If they can't breathe, cough or speak: five firm back blows between the shoulder blades, then five abdominal thrusts (fist above the navel, pull in and up), and repeat. If they collapse, start CPR. Infants get back blows and chest thrusts instead.

v.c: until it's out or they collapse

slides.h: Severe bleeding: press, and don't let go
slides.p: Direct, firm pressure with a cloth or your hands, straight onto the wound, for at least ten minutes without peeking. If it soaks through, add more on top. For a limb wound that won't stop, a tourniquet two to three inches above the wound, tightened until bleeding stops; note the time.

items: Press hard, directly on the wound
Don't lift to look; add layers
Limb still bleeding? Tourniquet high and tight, note the time

slides.h: Burns: cool water, not ice
slides.p: Run cool (not cold) water over the burn for 20 minutes; it limits damage even if you start late. Remove rings and watches before swelling. Don't use ice, butter or toothpaste; don't pop blisters. Cover loosely with cling film or a clean dry dressing. Face, hands, genitals, large or deep burns: hospital.

slides.h: Stroke and heart attack: the clock is the treatment
slides.p: Stroke: FAST. Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech slurred, Time to call 911; note when symptoms started. Heart attack: chest pressure, pain spreading to arm, jaw or back, sweating, breathlessness; women often get nausea or fatigue. Call, don't drive. Chew an aspirin if advised and not allergic.

slides.h: The recovery position, and a real course
slides.p: Someone unconscious but breathing: roll them onto their side, head tilted back, top knee bent, so the airway stays open and vomit drains. Then take a course. Four hours with a mannequin and an instructor makes all of this automatic, which is what counts when it's your kitchen.

items: A first-aid kit you've opened before
An AED location you know (work, gym)
A CPR/first-aid course every two years

quiz.q: The rate for chest compressions is…
quiz.why: 100 to 120 per minute, at least two inches deep, letting the chest fully recoil.

quiz.q: The first thing to do for a burn is…
a: Run cool water over it for 20 minutes
quiz.why: Cool running water limits the depth of the burn; ice damages tissue, and oils trap heat.

quiz.q: Someone is choking and cannot speak, cough or breathe. You should…
a: Alternate five back blows and five abdominal thrusts
Wait for it to clear on its own
quiz.why: Repeat until the object comes out. If they collapse, start CPR.

take: Call 911, start compressions at 100–120 a minute, send for the AED.
Choking: back blows and abdominal thrusts. Bleeding: hard, direct pressure.
Burns: cool water for 20 minutes. Stroke: FAST. Then take a real course.
src: American Red Cross: First aid steps
